concepts.name: TTLs and why invalidation is hard
Exact-match and semantic LLM response caches
Building a response cache in Redis

questions.prompt: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?

choices.text: The cache fetches the value from the database itself and returns it
The application reads the database, stores the value in the cache, and returns it
The request fails and the client retries once the cache is warm
The database pushes the value into the cache on its next write

questions.explanation: In cache-aside (lazy loading) the application is responsible for reading and writing storage; the cache never talks to the database. So a miss costs three trips: check the cache, read the database, write the cache. Only data someone asked for gets cached.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview.
sources.claim: In cache-aside the application looks in the cache, and on a miss loads the entry from the database, adds it to the cache and returns it; the cache does not interact with storage directly.

questions.prompt: Compared with cache-aside, what is the main trade-off of a write-through cache?

choices.text: Reads of just-written data are slow because they miss the cache, but writes return fast
Data can be lost if the cache fails before it has flushed the write to the database
It can never hold stale data, so it needs no TTL, eviction policy or invalidation at all
Writes are slower, as each waits on the database, and much cached data is never read

questions.explanation: In write-through the application writes to the cache, which synchronously writes to the database before returning. That makes writes slower but reads of freshly written data fast. Because everything written is cached, much of it may never be read, which a TTL helps limit. Data loss on cache failure is the risk of write-behind, which writes to the database asynchronously.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview.
sources.claim: Write-through writes synchronously to the database via the cache, so writes are slow and most data written may never be read (mitigated with a TTL), while write-behind risks data loss if the cache fails before flushing.

questions.prompt: A cache-aside cache stores user profiles with a 1-hour TTL. A user changes their name and the code updates only the database. What do other readers see?

choices.text: The old name, until the entry expires or the code deletes the key on write
The new name at once, because the cache notices database changes
An error, because the cache and database disagree
The new name, because the TTL restarts when the row changes

questions.explanation: In cache-aside the cache doesn't talk to the database, so it keeps serving the copy it has. The Primer notes the data can become stale when the database is updated, and a TTL only limits how long. To make changes visible sooner, delete (or update) the cache key whenever you write the database.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview.
sources.claim: A cache-aside entry can become stale if the database is updated, which a TTL limits and which write-through or explicit updates of the cache mitigate.

questions.prompt: Why is cache invalidation hard? Describe two ways a cache can serve wrong or slow results, and how you would limit each.

model_answer.summary: A cache is a copy of the source of truth, and keeping the copy consistent as data changes, under concurrency and failures, is where it goes wrong.
key_points: The cache must be kept consistent with the source of truth, such as the database
If a write updates the database but not the cache, readers get stale data until the entry expires
Delete or update the key on every write, and set a TTL to bound how stale data can get
Races: a slow reader can put an old value back into the cache after a writer deleted the key, so a TTL is still needed as a backstop
When a cache node fails, its replacement starts empty and every request misses, so latency rises until it warms up

questions.explanation: The Primer lists cache invalidation as a difficult problem with added complexity about when to update the cache. TTLs and delete-on-write don't make it perfect; they make the staleness bounded and predictable.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview.
sources.claim: The Primer lists as cache disadvantages the need to keep the cache consistent with the source of truth through invalidation, and that a new cache node starts empty so latency rises until it is warmed.

questions.prompt: You add an exact-match response cache in front of your LLM calls. What should the cache key be built from?

choices.text: The last user message only, so the same question in different conversations hits the cache
The user ID, so each user gets back their own previously cached answer
A hash of the full request: model, system prompt, messages, tools and sampling parameters
The request's timestamp rounded to the minute, so entries expire on their own

questions.explanation: An exact-match cache may only reuse a response when the whole request is identical. Keying on the last message alone would serve the same answer after a different system prompt, model or conversation history. Hash a canonical form of the full request, including the model version, so an upgrade doesn't return old answers.

sources.title: Redis semantic cache
sources.claim: Redis describes an exact-match cache as one that only hits when the query is byte-identical to a stored one.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Anthropic builds its cache prefix from tools, then system, then messages, and reuses it only when those segments are 100% identical, showing the whole request (not just the last message) determines reuse.

questions.prompt: Your semantic cache answered "How do I cancel my subscription?" with the cached answer to "How do I cancel my order?". What went wrong?

choices.text: The TTL was too long, so the cached answer had gone stale before it was served
The similarity threshold was too loose, so a different question counted as a match
The cache used exact string matching instead of comparing embeddings of the prompts
The provider's prompt cache returned a stale prefix from an earlier request

questions.explanation: A semantic cache embeds the prompt and reuses a stored answer when a past prompt is close enough. Redis calls threshold tuning the core difficulty: too loose and you serve wrong answers, too tight and the hit rate collapses. Adding hard filters, such as tenant, locale and model version, also keeps reuse within safe limits.

sources.title: Redis semantic cache
sources.claim: Redis calls threshold tuning the core difficulty of semantic caching (too loose serves wrong answers, too tight collapses hit rate) and recommends hard metadata filters such as tenant, locale and model version.

questions.prompt: What does provider-side prompt caching, such as Anthropic's `cache_control`, actually reuse?

choices.text: The processed prompt prefix; the model still generates a fresh response
The previous response, returned for an identical prompt
The embedding of the prompt, to find similar past answers
The output tokens, which are then billed at a discount

questions.explanation: Prompt caching stores the prompt prefix up to a cache breakpoint, in the order tools, then system, then messages. Later requests with the same prefix read it from the cache at a fraction of the input price, but the model still runs and produces a new response. It saves input cost and latency, not the whole call.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Prompt caching caches the prompt prefix in the order tools, system, messages; it has no effect on output generation, and cache reads are billed at a fraction (typically 0.1x) of the base input price.

questions.prompt: Your system prompt begins with `Current time: 14:03:27`, followed by 5,000 tokens of fixed instructions. The prompt cache never hits. Why?

choices.text: The prompt is too long: prompts over a few thousand tokens can't be cached
System prompts can't be cached; only the user and assistant messages can be
The default cache lifetime is under one second, so each entry expires before reuse
The cache needs an exact prefix match, and the timestamp changes it every request

questions.explanation: A cache hit needs the prefix up to the breakpoint to be identical. A changing value at the start makes every prefix new, so every request writes the cache and none reads it. Put stable content first and dynamic content, such as the time or the user's question, after the cached part. The default lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed each time the cache is used.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments up to and including the block marked with cache_control, and the default cache lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed each time it is used.

questions.prompt: Compare an exact-match response cache, a semantic cache and provider prompt caching for an LLM app. For each, say what it saves and what can go wrong.

model_answer.summary: Exact-match and semantic caches skip the LLM call entirely on a hit; prompt caching only makes the input cheaper and faster while the model still runs.
key_points: An exact-match cache returns a stored response only for a byte-identical request, so it is safe but has a low hit rate on varied questions
A semantic cache reuses answers for similar prompts using embeddings and a similarity threshold, so it hits on paraphrases
A semantic cache can return an answer to a different question if the threshold is too loose, so it needs tuning and metadata scoping
Provider prompt caching reuses the processed prompt prefix, cutting input cost and latency, but still runs the model on every call
Prompt caching doesn't change the response, while both response caches return an old answer that may be stale

questions.explanation: They solve different problems and can be combined: prompt caching for long, stable system prompts and tool definitions, an exact-match cache for repeated identical calls, and a carefully scoped semantic cache for FAQ-style traffic.

sources.title: Redis semantic cache
sources.claim: A semantic cache stores complete LLM responses and skips the LLM on a hit, exact-match caches only hit on byte-identical queries, and provider prompt caching discounts repeated prefixes but still runs the model on every call.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Prompt caching reuses the prompt prefix and does not change the generated response.

questions.prompt: A cached response was stored with `SET key value EX 3600`. Later, code refreshes it with plain `SET key newvalue`. What happens to its expiry?

choices.text: It keeps the remaining time from the first `SET`
It resets to a fresh 3600 seconds
The TTL is discarded, so the key never expires
Redis rejects the `SET` because the key has a TTL

questions.explanation: A successful `SET` discards any previous time to live. Without `EX` (or `KEEPTTL` to retain the old TTL), the refreshed key lives forever, and a cache that was meant to expire slowly fills memory. Always pass the TTL when you write a cache entry.

sources.title: SET
sources.claim: Any previous time to live on a key is discarded on a successful SET, EX sets an expiry in seconds, and KEEPTTL retains the existing TTL.

questions.prompt: Your Redis response cache keeps growing and some keys were written without a TTL. Which setting bounds its memory?

choices.text: Nothing: Redis limits memory to 3 GB by default on 64-bit systems
Set `maxmemory` and `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`, so the least recently used keys are evicted
Set `maxmemory-policy volatile-lru`, which evicts any key when memory runs out
Set `maxmemory-policy noeviction`, which removes expired keys sooner

questions.explanation: On 64-bit systems `maxmemory` defaults to 0, meaning no limit. With a limit set, `allkeys-lru` evicts the least recently used keys, and Redis calls it a good default for caches. `volatile-*` policies only evict keys that have a TTL and act like `noeviction` when none do; `noeviction` returns errors on writes instead of evicting.

sources.title: Key eviction
sources.claim: maxmemory 0 (no limit) is the default on 64-bit systems (32-bit has an implicit 3GB limit); allkeys-lru is a good default policy; volatile-* policies behave like noeviction when no keys have a TTL; noeviction returns errors on writes.

questions.prompt: Design the Redis response cache for identical requests to `agent-api`: the key, the value, the TTL, the read and write path, and what you would not cache.

model_answer.summary: Use cache-aside: key on a hash of the full request, store the serialized response with a TTL, check Redis before calling the LLM, and never cache failures.
key_points: The key is a prefix plus a hash of the canonical request: model, system prompt, messages, tools and parameters
The value is the serialized response, written with `SET key value EX <seconds>` so it expires
On each request check Redis first; on a miss call the LLM, store the result, then return it
Don't cache errors or incomplete responses, such as a stream that failed midway
Include the model version in the key so a model change doesn't serve old answers

questions.explanation: This is the lesson's exercise. It is cache-aside applied to LLM calls: the application owns both the lookup and the fill. The TTL keeps answers from going stale forever and caps memory together with an eviction policy.

sources.title: SET
sources.claim: SET key value EX seconds writes a value with an expiry in seconds, and a plain SET discards any previous TTL.
